questions.q:
Assertion (A): India is the seventh-largest country in the world.
Reason (R): The Himalayan Mountain range stands as a natural barrier in the north of India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the Himalayas being a barrier says nothing about the country's size, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Tara writes in her notebook: 'The Indian Subcontinent is a seventh continent, because seven countries are counted in it.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter calls it a subcontinent because it is part of the continent of Asia: India and its six neighbours form a region within Asia, not a continent of their own.
o: It is a region of seven countries lying within the continent of Asia, so it is not a continent
It is a continent only if the Himalayan range is counted as its seventh country
It is a separate continent, but one that has only six countries besides India
It is a name for the island group south of India, so the count of seven is wrong

questions.q: The chapter names seven countries in the Indian Subcontinent and six countries across which the Himalayan range stretches. The number of subcontinent countries that the range does NOT cross is ___.

The Himalayan range stretches across six countries: India, Nepal, Bhutan, China, Pakistan and Afghanistan. The Indian Subcontinent has seven countries: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. How many countries appear in both lists?
questions.a: India, Pakistan, Nepal and Bhutan are in both lists: four. China and Afghanistan are only Himalayan; Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Myanmar are only in the subcontinent.

questions.q: Leela says, 'India and the Indian Subcontinent are different, because the subcontinent is only India's six neighbours put together.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. She is right that they differ: India is one country, while the subcontinent is a larger region that is a part of Asia. She is wrong that it is only the six neighbours: the subcontinent counts India as well, so it has seven countries.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: India is one country and the subcontinent is a bigger region within Asia
Wrong part: India is included, so seven countries and six neighbours

questions.q: The legend of a physical map reads: green 0-200 m, yellow 200-500 m, brown 500-3,000 m, white above 3,000 m. Ritu marks a hill station at 1,800 m, a delta town at 15 m, a peak at 8,000 m and a plateau town at 450 m. Which list gives the colours of these four places in order?
questions.a: The chapter says the colours on the map show altitudes. 1,800 m is brown, 15 m green, 8,000 m white and 450 m yellow. The other lists swap the hill station with the plateau town, or the delta town with the plateau town, or the peak with the hill station.
o: brown, green, white, yellow
brown, yellow, white, green
yellow, green, white, brown
white, green, brown, yellow

questions.q: A student writes: 'India is the seventh-largest country, so it is the seventh country of the Indian Subcontinent, and it has seven neighbours there.' (a) Point out the two mistakes. (b) Give the correct numbers from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 'Seventh-largest' is India's rank by size among all the world's countries, not its position in the subcontinent; and the seven counts the subcontinent's countries with India included, so India has six neighbours, not seven. (b) Seventh-largest in the world; seven countries in the subcontinent counting India; six neighbours.
s: Part (a): the rank is by size in the world, not a place in the subcontinent, and seven includes India itself
Part (b): seventh-largest in the world, seven countries counting India, six neighbours

questions.q: A quiz-setter wants a clue whose answer is Myanmar and cannot be Afghanistan. Which clue works, going by the chapter?
questions.a: Myanmar is in the chapter's list of subcontinent neighbours; Afghanistan is not. The Himalayan clue picks out Afghanistan but not Myanmar, and 'a country of Asia' fits both.
o: It is one of the six neighbours that form the Indian Subcontinent with India
The Himalayan range stretches across it
It is a country of the continent of Asia
It is one of India's own island groups in the Indian Ocean

questions.q:
Match each number in Column A with what the chapter uses it for in Column B.
Column A: 1. seventh  2. seven  3. six  4. five
Column B: a. the regions into which India's land is divided for discussion  b. India's place among the world's countries by size  c. the countries of the Indian Subcontinent, counting India  d. India's neighbours that form the subcontinent with it
questions.a: 'Seventh' is India's rank by size among the world's countries; seven is the count of the subcontinent with India included; six is the neighbours alone; five is the regions. The distractors swap seven with six or seventh with seven.

questions.q: The chapter opens with Sri Aurobindo's words: 'To us, by its very geography, the country [India] appears to be quite distinct from other countries, and that itself gives it a certain national character.' (a) Name the three things the chapter says India's natural boundaries have played a crucial role in shaping. (b) A student argues that only the Himalayas make India distinct. Use the other boundary features to show why her argument is incomplete.
questions.a: (a) India's climate, culture and history. (b) The Thar Desert and Arabian Sea in the west, the Indian Ocean in the south and the Bay of Bengal in the east also bound India; the chapter says these features together create a separation between India and the rest of the continent, so the Himalayas are only the northern part.
s: Part (a): climate, culture and history
Part (b): names the western, southern and eastern boundary features and says all of them separate India from the rest of the continent

questions.q:
Read the statements about India's place and boundaries.
1. India is the seventh-largest country in the world and a part of Asia.
2. The Indian Subcontinent is called a subcontinent since it is part of the continent of Asia.
3. The Thar Desert and the Bay of Bengal together mark India's western limits.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are stated in the chapter. 3 is false: the Thar Desert and the Arabian Sea mark the western limits; the Bay of Bengal is the eastern boundary.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: True or False? 'Water forms India's natural boundary on every side.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Water bounds the south (Indian Ocean), east (Bay of Bengal) and, with the Thar Desert, the west (Arabian Sea). The north is bounded by a mountain range, the Himalayas, so not every side is water.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the north is the Himalayan Mountain range and the west also has the Thar Desert

questions.q: A map-maker proposes to shade nine countries - the seven of the Indian Subcontinent plus China and Afghanistan - and to label the whole patch 'Indian Subcontinent', because 'the Himalayan range runs through all of them'. Evaluate the proposal using the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter's subcontinent is India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, so China and Afghanistan are not in it. The map-maker's reason is also wrong: the range stretches across six countries (India, Nepal, Bhutan, China, Pakistan, Afghanistan), so it does not run through Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Myanmar. China and Afghanistan share the range with some of the seven, but that is a different grouping, the Himalayan countries. Verdict: reject the label; shade the seven, and mark the range's six countries separately if wanted.
s: Names the chapter's seven countries
China and Afghanistan are not among them
The range does not run through Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Myanmar, so the premise is false
The range's six countries are a different grouping from the subcontinent
Verdict: reject the label, with the corrected map

questions.q: A student claims: 'The chapter says India has exactly five kinds of land and nothing else.' (a) Using the chapter's wording, say why it refers to five regions. (b) Which sentence of the chapter shows she is going too far?
questions.a: (a) Often, for the purpose of discussion, we refer to five regions. (b) 'It would be difficult to go into all the details at this stage since India is large and diverse': the five regions are a convenient grouping, not a complete list of every kind of land.
s: Part (a): the five regions are used for the purpose of discussion
Part (b): points to the sentence saying it is difficult to give all details because India is large and diverse

questions.q: A class wants one picture for each of the chapter's five regions and has six candidates: Shimla, Jaisalmer, a paddy field in West Bengal, Munnar in Kerala, Lakshadweep and Gaumukh. (a) Place each candidate in its region. (b) Which region receives two candidates?
questions.a: (a) Shimla and Gaumukh: the great mountain zone; Jaisalmer: the desert region; the West Bengal paddy field: the plains of the Ganga and the Indus; Munnar: the southern peninsula; Lakshadweep: the islands. (b) The great mountain zone, with Shimla and Gaumukh.
s: Jaisalmer in the desert region, the paddy field in the plains, Munnar in the southern peninsula
Lakshadweep in the islands
The mountain zone receives two: Shimla and Gaumukh

questions.q: The Himalayan range appears in the chapter's list of natural boundaries and also in its list of five regions. (a) Under what name does the second list include it? (b) Explain the different job the range is given in each list.
questions.a: (a) The great mountain zone. (b) As a boundary it is a natural barrier in the north that separates India from the rest of the continent. As a region it is one of five zones used to describe the land of India itself.
s: Part (a): the great mountain zone
Part (b): barrier on the north edge versus one of five zones inside the country's land

questions.q:
A geography club in a Nagpur school has Rs 3,000 for wall panels titled 'Why India stands apart in Asia'. Panel prices: natural boundaries Rs 1,800; five regions Rs 1,500; neighbours of India Rs 900. The neighbours panel will list every country that forms the subcontinent with India, other than India itself.
(a) How many names will the neighbours panel list, and why does the chapter call this group a 'sub'continent?
(b) What must the boundaries panel show to explain why India appears 'quite distinct' from the rest of the continent?
(c) Which pairs of panels fit within the budget, and what does each pair cost?
(d) Recommend one affordable pair, justify it against the title, and name one thing the club gives up by choosing it.
questions.a: (a) Six (Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka, Myanmar); it is a part of the continent of Asia. (b) The Himalayas (north), Thar Desert and Arabian Sea (west), Indian Ocean (south) and Bay of Bengal (east), which separate India from the rest of the continent. (c) Boundaries + neighbours = Rs 2,700; regions + neighbours = Rs 2,400; boundaries + regions = Rs 3,300, over budget. (d) Boundaries + neighbours fits a title about standing apart, because the boundaries are what separate India; the club gives up the regions panel on variety inside India and Rs 300 of saving. (Regions + neighbours is accepted only if justified against the title, giving up the boundaries panel.)
s: Part (a): six countries, part of Asia
Part (b): natural boundary features and the separation they create
Part (c): Rs 2,700 and Rs 2,400 fit; Rs 3,300 does not
Part (d): a pair chosen against the title, with one named sacrifice

questions.q: India has been called a 'mini-continent'. Using the chapter's five regions, give three reasons why this name fits.
questions.a: Within one country it holds a great mountain zone, the Ganga-Indus plains, a desert region, a southern peninsula and islands; they differ in climate, soil, plants, animals and ways of living, as in different parts of a continent. The chapter says the diverse features created a variety of conditions.
s: Names at least three different regions inside India
Notes the variety in conditions such as soil, flora, fauna or life
Links the variety to the size and diversity of the country, as a continent has

questions.q: A new student says, 'India is just another country of Asia; nothing about where it lies sets it apart.' Using the chapter, argue against this. Cover: its size and place, the subcontinent it belongs to, the features that bound it, what those features have done, and the variety inside it.
questions.a: India is the seventh-largest country in the world and a part of Asia. With Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar it forms the Indian Subcontinent. The Himalayas bound it in the north, the Thar Desert and Arabian Sea in the west, the Indian Ocean in the south and the Bay of Bengal in the east, creating a separation from the rest of the continent. This separation has played a crucial role in shaping India's climate, culture and history. Inside, five regions (mountain zone, plains of the Ganga and the Indus, desert, southern peninsula, islands) show great variety.
s: Size and place: seventh-largest, part of Asia
Subcontinent with the six named neighbours
The boundary features on the four sides
They separate India and shaped climate, culture and history
Variety inside India shown by the five regions

questions.q:
In a school quiz the question was: 'Name the countries that, with India, form the Indian Subcontinent.' Team Kaveri wrote Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Team Narmada wrote those six and also Afghanistan and China. The quiz master gives 1 mark for each correct name and takes away 1 mark for each wrong name. Team Narmada appeals, saying the Himalayas also run through Afghanistan and China. The quiz master can (i) reject the appeal, or (ii) accept it and cancel Narmada's penalty.
(a) What marks does each team get at present?
(b) Which two names did Team Narmada add that are not in the chapter's list?
(c) Is the appeal's fact correct, and does it answer the question that was asked?
(d) Compare the final scores under (i) and (ii) and decide which the quiz master should choose, naming what the other choice would cost.
questions.a: (a) Kaveri 6; Narmada 6 - 2 = 4. (b) Afghanistan and China. (c) The fact is correct: the range stretches across six countries including China and Afghanistan. But the question asked for the subcontinent, whose members the chapter lists, so the fact answers a different question. (d) Under (i) Kaveri 6, Narmada 4; under (ii) both 6, a tie. Choose (i): the answer must fit the question asked, and (ii) would reward two wrong names and erase Kaveri's lead. The cost of (i) is that Narmada is penalised although its Himalayan fact is true.
s: Part (a): Kaveri 6, Narmada 4
Part (b): Afghanistan and China
Part (c): fact true, but it answers a different question
Part (d): (i) gives 6 and 4, (ii) a 6-6 tie; chooses (i) and names the cost

questions.q:
A museum in Dehradun has Rs 6 lakh for two new Himalaya galleries. Options: 'Water Tower of Asia' Rs 4 lakh, 'How the mountains were formed' Rs 3 lakh, 'Life in the ranges' Rs 2 lakh. A survey of 200 visitors found that 90 most want to know where the great rivers get their water, 70 want the story of how the mountains formed and 40 want to know how people and wildlife live in the mountains. Each visitor's first wish is served only if that gallery is built.
(a) Which pairs of galleries fit the Rs 6 lakh, and what does each cost?
(b) How many of the 200 visitors' first wishes does each affordable pair serve?
(c) The 'formation' gallery's draft panel says, 'The Himalayas stopped growing millions of years ago.' Correct it using the chapter's figures.
(d) Recommend a pair, and say what the museum gives up by choosing it rather than the other affordable pair.
questions.a: (a) Water Tower + Formation = Rs 7 lakh (over budget); Water Tower + Life = Rs 6 lakh; Formation + Life = Rs 5 lakh. (b) Water Tower + Life serves 90 + 40 = 130; Formation + Life serves 70 + 40 = 110. (c) India is still pushing into Asia at about five centimetres a year and the Himalayas are still rising about five millimetres a year, which adds up to five metres over a millennium. (d) Water Tower + Life: it serves 20 more visitors, at the cost of the whole Rs 6 lakh (Rs 1 lakh more than the other pair) and of the formation story. Choosing Formation + Life saves Rs 1 lakh but leaves the biggest group (90) unserved; either is acceptable only if the trade-off is stated.
s: Part (a): Rs 6 lakh and Rs 5 lakh pairs fit; Rs 7 lakh does not
Part (b): 130 and 110 visitors
Part (c): still pushing 5 cm a year, still rising 5 mm a year, 5 m in a millennium
Part (d): a pair chosen with the visitor-versus-cost trade-off stated

questions.q: The chapter says India is still pushing into Asia at about 5 centimetres a year, while the Himalayas rise only about 5 millimetres a year. How many times larger is the yearly push than the yearly rise?
questions.a: 5 cm = 50 mm, and 50 mm divided by 5 mm is 10 times. Not 100 (that would be 5 cm against 0.5 mm) and not 1 (units were not matched).
o: 10 times
100 times
1 time (they are equal)
5 times

questions.q: Meena's notes say: 'India collided with Eurasia first, and only after that did it break away from Gondwana and start moving north.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter's order is: part of Gondwana (neighbour Africa), broke away, moved north, reached Eurasia about 50 million years ago, collided; the land between crumpled and rose. Meena has put the collision before the break-away.
o: India first broke away from Gondwana, where Africa was its neighbour, and moved north; the collision with Eurasia about 50 million years ago came later
India was never part of a larger landmass; it collided with Eurasia where it now stands, about 50 million years ago
India broke away from Eurasia about 50 million years ago and moved south, which crumpled the land
The land between India and Eurasia crumpled first, and that push moved India away from Gondwana

questions.q: Anil says, 'At the rates in the chapter, in 2,000 years India will have pushed about 100 metres further into Asia, and the Himalayas will have risen about 10 metres.' Is he right? Check both figures.
questions.a: Yes. India pushes about 5 cm a year: 5 x 2,000 = 10,000 cm = 100 m. The Himalayas rise about 5 mm a year: 5 x 2,000 = 10,000 mm = 10 m. Both of Anil's figures follow from the chapter's rates, assuming the rates stay the same.
s: Verdict: right
India's push: 5 cm x 2,000 = 100 m with the unit conversion shown
Himalayan rise: 5 mm x 2,000 = 10 m with the unit conversion shown

questions.q: True or False? 'Hill stations such as Shimla and Mussoorie lie in the Himadri, because its moderate climate suits human habitation.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The hill stations lie in the Himachal (Lower Himalayas), whose climate is more moderate. The Himadri is the highest and most rugged part, snow-covered throughout the year, with few human settlements.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: hill stations and the moderate climate belong to the Himachal; the Himadri is snow-covered and thinly settled

questions.q: A geology student photographs sharply bent, folded layers of rock high in the Himalayas. Which event does the chapter give as the cause of such folding?
questions.a: The chapter says the land between India and Eurasia crumpled and rose when they collided, like a carpet wrinkling; Fig. 1.5 shows the folded layers. Dunes, deltas and snowmelt are not mountain-folding processes.
o: India collided with Eurasia and the land between them crumpled and rose
Wind shifted loose sand into hill-like formations
A river deposited sediments where it met a larger water body
Summer snowmelt wore the rock into folds as it fed the rivers

questions.q:
Read the statements about the formation of the Himalayas.
1. India reached the landmass of Eurasia and collided with it about 50 million years ago.
2. India is still pushing into Asia today, at about five millimetres each year.
3. The Himalayas are still rising by about five millimetres each year, which adds up to five metres over a millennium.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are stated in the chapter. 2 is false: India pushes at about five centimetres a year; five millimetres is the yearly rise of the Himalayas.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) Give the two Sanskrit words that make up 'Himalaya' and their meanings. (b) Show how the name fits two facts the chapter gives: the Himadri is snow-covered throughout the year, and the summer melting of Himalayan snow feeds major rivers.
questions.a: (a) Hima means 'snow' and alaya means 'abode' or 'dwelling'. (b) 'Abode of snow' fits the Himadri, where snow stays all year; and because that snow melts in summer into the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra, the range is also called the 'Water Tower of Asia'.
s: Part (a): hima = snow, alaya = abode or dwelling
Part (b): the all-year snow of the Himadri fits 'abode of snow', and its summer melt feeds the rivers

questions.q:
Neha's diary of a journey north from the plains: Day 1 - 'rolling low hills with dense forests and plenty of wildlife'; Day 2 - 'a hill station with a moderate climate and many families'; Day 3 - 'rugged peaks under snow in every month, hardly any village'.
(a) Name the range she reaches on each day.
(b) What do the three days show about how the height of the land changes as she goes north?
(c) Why does the chapter call the Day 1 range a transition zone?
(d) Which day's range can support the fewest settlements, and why?
questions.a: (a) Day 1 Shivalik Hills (Outer Himalayas); Day 2 Himachal (Lower Himalayas); Day 3 Himadri (Greater Himalayas). (b) The land gets higher going north: Shivalik lowest and outermost, then the Himachal, then the Himadri, the highest and most rugged. (c) The Shivalik Hills lie between the Himalayas and the Gangetic (Northern) Plains. (d) The Himadri: it is snow-covered throughout the year, rugged, and life there is tough, so there are not many settlements.
s: Part (a): Shivalik, Himachal, Himadri in order
Part (b): height rises northwards from the lowest Shivalik to the highest Himadri
Part (c): Shivalik is the transition zone between the Himalayas and the Gangetic Plains
Part (d): Himadri, because snow all year and tough life leave few settlements

questions.q: A mountaineering club lists four Himalayan peaks by height: P 7,820 m, Q 8,091 m, R 8,586 m and S 7,992 m. Which of them are 'Eight Thousanders' by the chapter's description?
questions.a: The chapter calls peaks over 8000 metres the 'Eight Thousanders'. Only Q (8,091 m) and R (8,586 m) are over 8,000 m; S at 7,992 m falls just short.
o: Q and R only
P, Q and R only
Q, R and S only
R only

questions.q: Aarav travels by road from the plains of Uttarakhand into the mountains. First he passes rolling, forested hills, then reaches a hill station such as Nainital, and finally sees snow peaks that stay white all year. Which order of ranges did he cross?
questions.a: The rolling forested outer hills are the Shivalik; the hill stations are in the Himachal; the year-round snow peaks are the Himadri. So he crossed Shivalik, Himachal, Himadri.
o: Shivalik, Himachal, Himadri
Himachal, Shivalik, Himadri
Himadri, Himachal, Shivalik
Shivalik, Himadri, Himachal

questions.q: A trekker at Gaumukh in Uttarakhand says, 'This is where the Ganga itself begins.' (a) Which river originates at Gaumukh, and at the edge of which glacier? (b) The chapter's box asks readers to remember, next time they see the Ganga, that 'its journey began there'. Does the chapter back the trekker's remark or correct it? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The Bhagirathi, a major tributary of the Ganga, originates at Gaumukh ('Cow's Mouth'), at the edge of the Gangotri Glacier. (b) It backs the spirit of the remark: the chapter itself says the Ganga's journey began there, while naming the Bhagirathi as the major tributary that begins at the spot.
s: Part (a): Bhagirathi, at the edge of the Gangotri Glacier
Part (b): the chapter says the Ganga's journey began there, through its tributary the Bhagirathi, so it backs the remark

questions.q: 'The Himalayas matter far beyond the mountains themselves.' Justify this statement with the water they supply, their meaning for people and their wildlife.
questions.a: Snowmelt feeds the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra, which give water for drinking, farming and industry to hundreds of millions, hence 'Water Tower of Asia'. The mountains are sacred, with temples and monasteries that draw monks and seekers. The Great Himalayan National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, protects diverse flora and fauna.
s: Water: snowmelt feeds the three major rivers
Culture and belief: sacred mountains, temples, monasteries
Biodiversity: Great Himalayan National Park, UNESCO site
Draws the conclusion that the range matters to millions beyond the mountains

questions.q: A pamphlet says, 'The rocks of the Himalayas have stayed in the same place since India was joined to Africa, because land never moves.' Show using the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says India was part of Gondwana, with Africa as its neighbour, then broke away and moved north. About 50 million years ago it collided with Eurasia and the land between crumpled and rose. India is still pushing into Asia today, so land does move.
s: Gondwana: India broke away from Africa's side and moved north
Collision about 50 million years ago made the land crumple and rise
India still pushes into Asia today, so the claim fails

questions.q: A student proposes that the Great Himalayan National Park, home to the Himalayan monal and the snow leopard, should be protected by the government alone, with the village communities moved out. Which fact from the chapter makes this proposal questionable?
questions.a: The chapter says the government and the village communities living inside the park both preserve its biodiversity. The UNESCO status does not bar communities, and the last option invents a range limit.
o: The park's biodiversity is being preserved by the government as well as the village communities that live inside it
The park is in Himachal Pradesh, where the Beas river flows through it
The park has been declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO, so only the government may enter it
The snow leopard and the monal are found only in the Himadri, where no one lives

questions.q: A builder from the plains proposes to replace the traditional kath-kuni houses of a western Himalayan village with thin plain-brick walls. (a) Which materials does the kath-kuni method combine? (b) Which two benefits of the traditional method would the builder's walls have to match?
questions.a: (a) Locally available stone and wood. (b) It keeps the house warm and resists damage in the event of mild earthquakes.
s: Part (a): locally available stone and wood
Part (b): keeps the house warm and resists damage in mild earthquakes

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Himalayas are sometimes called the 'Water Tower of Asia'.
Reason (R): In summer the snow on the mountains melts and feeds major rivers such as the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both true, and the snowmelt feeding the rivers is exactly why the Himalayas are called a water tower.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A school wall called 'The Himalayas and belief' needs three lines of text from the chapter. (a) What do the temples and monasteries built within the mountains show about how they are regarded? (b) Which glacier does the chapter call sacred, and what does it attract? (c) Who else comes to the mountains, and to do what?
questions.a: (a) The mountains themselves are considered sacred. (b) The Gangotri Glacier, which attracts many pilgrims. (c) Monks and spiritual seekers from around the world come to pray and meditate.
s: Mountains are considered sacred, with temples and monasteries built within them
Gangotri Glacier is sacred and attracts many pilgrims
Monks and spiritual seekers from around the world come to pray and meditate

questions.q: The chapter notes that the Brahmaputra 'gets bigger during summer instead of drying up'. (a) Using the chapter's account of the Himalayas, explain why. (b) Name the other two rivers fed in the same way and give one use of the water of these rivers.
questions.a: (a) In summer the snow on the mountains melts and feeds the river, so its water grows. (b) The Ganga and the Indus; their water is used for drinking, farming and industry.
s: Part (a): summer snowmelt from the Himalayas feeds it
Part (b): Ganga and Indus, with a use such as drinking, farming or industry

questions.q:
The table gives the monthly flow (in invented units of water per second) of a Himalayan river that irrigates the plains: January 120, March 180, May 640, July 910, September 520, November 150. A canal authority is deciding between (i) a reservoir costing Rs 12 crore that stores July water and serves 3 lakh people through the dry months, and (ii) shifting sowing to May-September at no cost, which would leave winter land idle and lose Rs 150 per person per year of winter income.
(a) Which month has the greatest flow, and in which season does the chapter say Himalayan snow melts to feed such rivers?
(b) How many times larger is the July flow than the January flow, to one decimal place?
(c) What is the reservoir's cost per person, and in how many years would the lost winter income under (ii) equal that cost?
(d) Which option would you advise, and what is the risk of your choice?
questions.a: (a) July; the chapter says the snow melts in summer. (b) 910 / 120 = 7.6 times. (c) Rs 12 crore / 3 lakh = Rs 400 per person; 400 / 150 = about 2.7 years. (d) If the plan will run for more than about three years, the reservoir is cheaper per person than the lost income and gives water in the dry months; the risk is the large up-front cost and dependence on summer snowmelt filling it. Option (ii) is better only for a very short horizon, and it leaves winter land idle. Either is acceptable if the break-even of about 2.7 years is used.
s: Part (a): July, in summer
Part (b): 910 / 120 = 7.6 times
Part (c): Rs 400 per person; about 2.7 years
Part (d): decision tied to the break-even and a named risk

questions.q:
Students of a Chennai school plan a stall called 'Ladakh Day' to show how a cold desert differs from a hot one. They have Rs 7,200 and room for two displays. Prices: the winter cold (a thermometer wall with the -30 degrees C winters) Rs 4,500; the salty lake (a model of Pangong Tso) Rs 3,000; the yaks (a puppet show) Rs 2,500.
(a) Why is Ladakh called a desert although it is so cold?
(b) What must the lake display say about the cause of the salty water?
(c) Which pairs of displays fit the Rs 7,200, and what does each pair cost?
(d) Choose a pair, justify it against the stall's aim, and name what you give up.
questions.a: (a) Because it receives very little rainfall. (b) Minerals dissolve from the surrounding mountain areas into the lake. (c) Cold + lake = Rs 7,500 (over); cold + yaks = Rs 7,000; lake + yaks = Rs 5,500. (d) Cold + yaks suits the aim of contrast with a hot desert and shows how families live, but gives up the lake and leaves only Rs 200; lake + yaks saves Rs 1,700 and explains a Ladakh feature, but gives up the cold-winter contrast. Either is acceptable if tied to the aim.
s: Part (a): very little rainfall
Part (b): minerals dissolving from surrounding mountains
Part (c): Rs 7,000 and Rs 5,500 fit; Rs 7,500 does not
Part (d): a pair chosen against the aim, with a named sacrifice

questions.q: True or False? 'Although the folded land of Ladakh was once part of an ocean, the chapter explains Pangong Tso's salty water by minerals dissolved from the surrounding mountain areas.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says the lake is salty because of the minerals that dissolve from the surrounding mountain areas; the ocean past of the folded land is used to explain why the rocks are largely sand and clay.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: salt comes from dissolved minerals; the ocean past explains the sand-and-clay rocks

questions.q: A weather note describes three places. X: winter nights below -30 degrees C, very little rainfall, rocky valleys. Y: very hot days, cold nights, very little rainfall, sand dunes. Z: mild winters and heavy rainfall. Going by the chapter's use of the word 'desert', which of them can be called deserts?
questions.a: The chapter says a desert need not be hot: Ladakh, with winters below -30 degrees C and very little rainfall, is a cold desert, and the Thar is a hot one. Z, with heavy rain, is neither. 'Y only' is the 'desert means hot' slip.
o: X and Y
Y only
Y and Z
X and Z

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Ladakh is a cold desert.
Reason (R): The rocks of Ladakh's folded mountains are made largely of sand and clay.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The rocks are a fact about the terrain, but Ladakh is a desert because of very little rainfall, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A railway planner is asked why new lines should be laid across the Gangetic Plains rather than the rocky land of Ladakh. Give three reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: The plains are flat, which has already allowed an elaborate road and rail network; a large proportion of India's population lives there; the fertile, river-fed land produces abundant farm goods to carry. Ladakh has rocky terrain and deep valleys.
s: Flat land suits roads and railways
Large population lives in the plains
Fertile land and rivers support farming and trade

questions.q: A forest officer notes two animals of the Gangetic Plains that were on the verge of extinction: the tiger and the Indian gharial. Which pair of safeguards matches the chapter?
questions.a: The captions say Project Tiger has supported the return of the tiger, and that laws prohibit harming or hunting the gharial. The swapped option reverses them.
o: Project Tiger has supported the tiger's return; laws prohibit harming or hunting the gharial
Laws prohibit harming or hunting the tiger; Project Tiger has supported the gharial's return
Both are protected only because they live in Bandhavgarh National Park
Neither needs protection, since the fertile plains give wildlife enough food

questions.q: A traveller leaves a Ladakh winter night at -32 degrees C and, after a flight, stands in the Thar on a day when the temperature is 46 degrees C. The rise in temperature she feels is ___ degrees C.
Rohan says, 'The Gangetic Plains are fertile and crowded partly because of mountains far away to the north.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. The Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra rivers originate in the Himalayas; with their tributaries they bring water and minerals that enrich the soil, making the plains highly fertile and ideal for agriculture, and a large proportion of India's population lives there.
s: Verdict: right
Rivers originate in the Himalayas and bring minerals and water
Fertile soil and agriculture support a large population

questions.q: Compare the cold desert of Ladakh and the Gangetic Plains under rainfall or water, terrain, farming and life of the people, and analyse why one supports far more people.
questions.a: Ladakh: very little rainfall, winter below -30 degrees C, rocky terrain and deep valleys, yaks for livelihood; few people. Plains: Himalayan rivers bring water and minerals, flat land, fertile soil, abundant farming, transport; a large share of India's population. A large share of India's population lives in the plains because of the fertile land and water, while Ladakh's cold, little rain and rocky terrain make life depend on animals like the yak.
s: Ladakh's climate and terrain described
Plains' water, soil and flat land described
Contrast in farming or livelihood (yaks vs agriculture)
Analysis: links resources to population

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with its cause in Column B, as the chapter gives it.
Column A: 1. Ladakh's rocks are made largely of sand and clay  2. Ladakh's mountains stand carved into odd shapes  3. The soil of the Northern Plains is highly fertile  4. Long road and rail lines cross the Northern Plains
Column B: a. rivers from the Himalayas bring minerals to the soil  b. the folded portion was once part of an ocean  c. wind and rain have eroded the mountains  d. the land is flat
questions.a: Sand and clay come from the ocean past; the odd shapes from erosion by wind and rain; fertile soil from river-borne minerals; the transport network from flat land. The distractors swap the ocean past with erosion, or the minerals with flat land.

questions.q: A tourist brochure says: 'Visit Ladakh in December for sunny sand dunes and warm days - a typical hot desert!' (a) Correct two claims in it using the chapter. (b) What does the chapter call such a region?
questions.a: (a) Winter temperatures in Ladakh drop below -30 degrees C, so the days are not warm; and the landscape is rugged, with rocky terrain, deep valleys and lakes, not sand dunes. (b) A cold desert.
s: Part (a): winters below -30 degrees C, and rocky terrain with deep valleys instead of dunes
Part (b): a cold desert

questions.q: A night-time satellite image shows dense clusters of lights over the Gangetic Plains and only scattered lights over Ladakh. Which fact from the chapter helps explain the difference?
questions.a: The chapter says a large proportion of India's population lives in the plains. The other options are invented: the Pangong Tso is a single lake, the plains are flat rather than rugged, and no link to the Arabian Sea is made.
o: A large proportion of India's population lives in the Gangetic Plains
The rivers of Ladakh are too salty to be used for electricity
The Gangetic Plains lie closer to the Arabian Sea than Ladakh does
The Gangetic Plains are rugged hills with many monasteries

questions.q:
Read the statements about Ladakh and the Northern Plains.
1. Ladakh's winter temperatures drop below -30 degrees C, yet it receives plenty of rainfall.
2. A large proportion of India's population lives in the Gangetic Plains.
3. The Ganga, the Brahmaputra and other rivers have been used for millennia for travel and trade.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: Ladakh receives very little rainfall, which is why it is a desert. 2 and 3 are stated in the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A farmer in Uttar Pradesh grows several crops on one field in a year (multi-cropping). (a) Which two things that the Himalayan rivers bring to the plains make this possible? (b) Which two features of Ladakh would make the same farming hard?
questions.a: (a) Water and minerals that enrich the soil and make it highly fertile. (b) Very little rainfall, and rocky terrain with deep valleys (also winters below -30 degrees C).
s: Part (a): water and soil-enriching minerals from the rivers
Part (b): very little rainfall and rocky terrain or deep valleys

questions.q: Suppose the Himalayas did not exist. Using the chapter, discuss what would happen to the rivers, farming and population of the Gangetic Plains.
questions.a: The Himalayas feed the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra with snowmelt, which is why they are the 'Water Tower of Asia'. Without them the rivers would lose their source and the minerals they bring would no longer enrich the soil, so the plains would not stay highly fertile. Farming and electricity from the rivers would suffer, and the large share of India's population that depends on the plains would lose water and food.
s: Himalayan snowmelt feeds the three river systems
Minerals carried by rivers enrich the soil, which would be lost
Farming and electricity would suffer
Large population depends on the plains
Reaches a clear conclusion

questions.q: A teacher asks what Pangong Tso's saltiness and the Gangetic Plains' fertility have in common according to the chapter. Which answer is correct?
questions.a: Pangong Tso is salty from minerals dissolved from the surrounding mountains, and the plains are fertile because rivers from the Himalayas bring minerals to the soil. The ocean past explains Ladakh's sand-and-clay rocks, and erosion explains its shapes.
o: In both, minerals carried from the mountains by water play the main part
In both, the land having once been part of an ocean is the main cause
In both, wind and rain eroding the mountains is the main cause
In both, very high daytime temperatures are the main cause

questions.q: Write two riddles, one whose answer is 'Ladakh' and one whose answer is 'the Gangetic Plains'. Give each riddle two clues from the chapter, and make sure no clue could fit the other region.
questions.a: E.g. Ladakh: 'My winter nights fall below -30 degrees C and little rain falls on my rocky terrain; my lake Pangong Tso is salty.' Gangetic Plains: 'Rivers from the Himalayas carry minerals to my soil; a large part of India's population lives on my flat land with its roads and railways.'
s: Riddle for Ladakh with two correct chapter clues
Riddle for the Gangetic Plains with two correct chapter clues
No clue fits both regions

questions.q: Kavya says, 'The rivers of the Northern Plains are useful only for drinking and farming.' (a) Name two other uses of these rivers that the chapter mentions. (b) Which use of these rivers does the chapter say has gone on for millennia?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: generating electricity, industrial use, travel and trade. (b) Travel and trade.
s: Part (a): two valid further uses such as electricity, industry or travel and trade
Part (b): travel and trade have gone on for millennia

questions.q: Heavy snow has closed the roads to a Ladakhi village for the winter. (a) List the uses of the yak that the chapter gives. (b) Which of them could meet the family's need for food, for clothing and for carrying goods, one use for each need?
questions.a: (a) Milk, meat, wool, dung and transport. (b) Food: milk or meat; clothing: wool; carrying goods: transport.
s: Part (a): milk, meat, wool, dung and transport
Part (b): matches food (milk or meat), clothing (wool) and carrying goods (transport)

questions.q:
A panchayat in the Gangetic Plains has Rs 30 lakh and can fund only one project. Project P: a small river-powered generator costing Rs 30 lakh, which would supply 1,500 households. Project Q: a loading yard beside the railway line costing Rs 24 lakh, which would let 800 farmers send their produce to distant markets.
(a) Which feature of the plains has allowed the road and railway networks that Project Q depends on?
(b) What does the chapter say about the rivers that supports Project P?
(c) Work out the cost per household for P and the cost per farmer for Q.
(d) Choose one project, justify it, and say which group is left waiting.
questions.a: (a) The flat land of the Northern Plains. (b) The rivers are also a source for generating electricity. (c) P: Rs 30,00,000 / 1,500 = Rs 2,000 per household; Q: Rs 24,00,000 / 800 = Rs 3,000 per farmer. (d) P reaches more people at a lower cost each and uses the rivers; Q costs Rs 6 lakh less in all and lets the fertile land's produce reach markets. Choosing P leaves the 800 farmers waiting; choosing Q leaves 1,500 households without new power. Either is acceptable if the trade-off is stated.
s: Part (a): flat land
Part (b): rivers are a source of electricity
Part (c): Rs 2,000 per household and Rs 3,000 per farmer
Part (d): a project chosen with the group left waiting named

questions.q: Two traders must cross the Thar on foot, one at noon and one at midnight. According to the chapter, which hardship do both of them still face?
questions.a: The chapter lists very high daytime temperatures, cold nights, and a lack of access to water as the conditions that deter movement. The first belongs to the noon trader only and the second to the midnight trader only; lack of water affects both. Dunes rise to about 150 m, far below the Aravallis' peaks.
o: A lack of access to water
Very high temperatures
Cold nights
Sand dunes as high as the Aravallis

questions.q: True or False? 'Taanka or kunds are channels that bring river water to Rajasthan's desert villages.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter describes taanka or kunds as special water collection systems that store rainwater, often for drinking; they are not channels carrying river water.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they store rainwater

questions.q:
A Delhi school plans a one-day visit for 40 students to study 'How people used the Aravalli Hills'. The grant is Rs 36,000. Site A is the Zawar mines at Rs 700 per student. Site B is the Chittorgarh fort at Rs 500 per student. Only one site can be visited.
(a) Name two minerals of the Aravallis and say what they have supported for centuries.
(b) What does the evidence from the Zawar mines show?
(c) What does each site cost for 40 students, and how much of the grant is left?
(d) Choose a site for the study aim, and say what the school gives up.
questions.a: (a) Any two of marble, granite, zinc, copper; they have supported mining and construction activities for centuries. (b) Over eight centuries ago Indians were the first in the world to master the extraction of zinc. (c) A: 40 x 700 = Rs 28,000, leaving Rs 8,000; B: 40 x 500 = Rs 20,000, leaving Rs 16,000. (d) Zawar answers 'how people used the hills' through mining and early zinc extraction; Chittorgarh shows another use, a fort whose hill location deterred the enemy, and leaves Rs 8,000 more. Either is acceptable if the sacrifice is named.
s: Part (a): two minerals; mining and construction
Part (b): early mastery of zinc extraction
Part (c): Rs 28,000 and Rs 20,000; Rs 8,000 and Rs 16,000 left
Part (d): a site chosen for the aim, with the sacrifice named

questions.q: Rohit photographs the same dune near Jaisalmer on two visits a month apart and sees that its crest has moved. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says dunes form when the wind shifts and shapes the sand into hill-like formations, so a dune of loose sand can move. Rock folding, river deposits and rainwater tanks do not shape dunes.
o: The wind keeps shifting the loose sand
The rock beneath it is slowly folding
A river is depositing sediment on it
Rainwater stored in kunds is washing it away

questions.q: (a) The Aravallis are some 2.5 billion years old, while the Himalayas began to rise when India collided with Eurasia about 50 million years ago. How many times older are the Aravallis? (b) The chapter says that over eight centuries ago Indians were the first in the world to master zinc extraction at Zawar. Taking 2026 as the present year, before which year did this happen?
questions.a: (a) 2,500 million / 50 million = 50 times. (b) 2026 - 800 = 1226, so before about the year 1226.
s: Part (a): 2.5 billion divided by 50 million is 50 times
Part (b): 2026 minus 800 gives before about 1226

questions.q: Vikram says, 'The Thar is a natural barrier because of its harsh conditions, so nobody can live there.' Is he right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. He is right that the Thar is a natural barrier: very high daytime temperatures, cold nights and a lack of access to water deter human and animal movement. He is wrong that nobody lives there: people have adapted their food habits, clothing and lifestyle, and Jaisalmer, the 'Golden City', stands in the middle of the desert.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: harsh conditions deter movement, so it is a barrier
Wrong part: people live there, having adapted their way of life

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Thar and the Aravallis.
1. Most of the Thar lies within India, spanning Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana.
2. The Aravallis span Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab.
3. Evidence from the ancient mines at Zawar shows that Indians were the first in the world to master the extraction of copper.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is stated in the chapter. 2 is false: the Aravallis span Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat; Punjab is in the Thar's list. 3 is false: the Zawar evidence is about zinc.
o: 1 only
2 only
3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: The tallest dunes of the Thar rise as high as 150 m, while Mount Abu, the highest peak of the Aravallis, towers over 1700 m. Roughly how many times as tall as the tallest dune is Mount Abu?
questions.a: 1700 / 150 is about 11.3, and Mount Abu is over 1700 m, so it is more than 11 times as tall. The other figures come from slips of a decimal place or of the division.
o: More than 11 times
About 5 times
About 2 times
More than 110 times

questions.q: A student's note reads: 'Jaisalmer Fort, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is one of the hill forts of the Aravallis.' (a) Correct the mistake using the chapter. (b) Name two forts that the chapter does place in the Aravallis.
questions.a: (a) Jaisalmer, the 'Golden City', lies in the middle of the Thar Desert, not in the Aravallis. (b) Any two of Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh and Ranthambore.
s: Part (a): Jaisalmer Fort is in the Thar Desert
Part (b): two of Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore

questions.q: The chapter says a drive of about 4 and a half hours takes us from Mount Abu in the Aravallis to Jodhpur in the Thar Desert, 'a drive into a completely different geography'. Compare the two places and analyse why the Aravallis matter for the land around Jodhpur. Cover the hills' age and height, the desert's conditions, the Aravallis' barrier role, and how people use each.
questions.a: Aravallis: among the oldest mountains, some 2.5 billion years old; Mount Abu over 1700 m, most hills 300-900 m; rich in marble, granite, zinc and copper; forts like Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh. Thar: a vast arid region with dunes up to 150 m; very high daytime temperatures, cold nights and scarce water; people adapt, for example by scouring utensils with sand and storing rainwater. The Aravallis act as a natural barrier that stops the Thar from expanding further eastward.
s: Aravallis' age and height described
Thar's conditions described
The barrier role of the Aravallis against the eastward spread of the Thar
How people use the hills (mining, forts)
How people live in the desert (water saving, storage)

questions.q: The chapter says the Thar spans Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana, and asks readers to find Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat as the states the Aravallis span. Which state is in the first list but not the second?
questions.a: Punjab is in the Thar's list only. Delhi is in the Aravalli list only; Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat are in both.
o: Punjab
Delhi
Haryana
Gujarat

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the Thar Desert, utensils are traditionally cleaned by scouring them with sand.
Reason (R): Water is scarce in the desert and women often travel long distances to fetch it.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and scarcity of water is the reason sand is used and only a little water kept for rinsing.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A Thar village of 40 households stores rainwater for drinking in taanka or kunds. (a) If each household uses 20 litres a day, how many litres does the village use daily? (b) For how many days will a full store of 36,000 litres last?
s: Part (a): 800 litres a day

questions.q: A student writes, 'The Aravallis are young mountains like the Himalayas, still rising every year.' Show using the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: The chapter says the Aravallis are among the oldest mountains in the world, some 2.5 billion years old. The rising of about five millimetres a year is described for the Himalayas, which began to rise only when India collided with Eurasia about 50 million years ago. So the Aravallis cannot be young.
s: Aravallis are among the oldest mountains in the world, about 2.5 billion years old
The Himalayas rose when India collided with Eurasia about 50 million years ago and still rise about 5 mm a year
Concludes that the claim confuses the two ranges

questions.q: A surveyor measures a hill in the Aravalli range at 1,300 m. Using the chapter, which statement about it is correct?
questions.a: The chapter says Mount Abu, the highest peak, towers over 1700 m, while most hills are between 300 and 900 m. A 1,300 m hill is above that usual band but below Mount Abu.
o: It is taller than most Aravalli hills but lower than Mount Abu
It is the highest peak of the range, since it is over 1,000 m
It is typical of the range, since most Aravalli hills are 900 to 1,700 m
It cannot belong to the range, because Aravalli hills stop at 900 m

questions.q: In the Thar, utensils are scoured with sand and only a little water is used for a light rinse. (a) Why is this the traditional method? (b) What is done with the rinse water, and what does that show about the way the people treat water?
questions.a: (a) Water is scarce in the desert and women often travel long distances every day to fetch it. (b) It is reused, for example for watering a plant, which shows that every drop is valued.
s: Part (a): water is scarce and has to be fetched over long distances
Part (b): rinse water is reused for a plant; water is valued

questions.q: Isha says, 'The Aravallis stop the Thar from spreading east, so no part of Haryana can belong to the desert.' Is she right? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The Aravallis prevent the desert from expanding further eastward, but the Thar already spans Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana. Stopping further spread is not the same as removing the desert from a state.
s: Verdict: not right
Aravallis prevent further eastward spread of the Thar
The Thar spans Rajasthan, Gujarat, Punjab and Haryana, so Haryana has desert

questions.q:
The Rajasthan tourism board has funds for one festival. Festival H, in the Jaisalmer fort town in the middle of the Thar, would cost Rs 90 lakh and draw 60,000 visitors. Festival K, at Kumbhalgarh in the Aravallis, would cost Rs 72 lakh and draw 40,000 visitors. Planners allow 5 litres of water per visitor per day for 3 days.
(a) What does the chapter say about water in the Thar, and what name does it give Jaisalmer?
(b) What is the cost per visitor of each festival?
(c) How many litres of water does each festival need?
(d) Recommend one festival and justify it, naming the cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Water is scarce in the desert and women often travel long distances to fetch it; Jaisalmer is the 'Golden City'. (b) H: Rs 90,00,000 / 60,000 = Rs 150; K: Rs 72,00,000 / 40,000 = Rs 180. (c) H: 60,000 x 5 x 3 = 9,00,000 litres; K: 40,000 x 5 x 3 = 6,00,000 litres. (d) H is cheaper per visitor but needs 3,00,000 litres more of scarce desert water; K costs Rs 30 more per visitor but eases the demand on the Thar. Either is acceptable if the cost (money or water) is named.
s: Part (a): water scarce, long trips to fetch it; the Golden City
Part (b): Rs 150 and Rs 180 per visitor
Part (c): 9,00,000 and 6,00,000 litres
Part (d): a festival chosen with its cost named

questions.q: A bus leaves Mount Abu in the Aravallis at 6:30 a.m. for Jodhpur; the chapter says the drive takes about 4 and a half hours. When and in what kind of landscape does it arrive?
questions.a: 6:30 a.m. plus 4 hours 30 minutes is 11:00 a.m., and the chapter says this drive takes us from the Aravallis into the Thar Desert, 'a completely different geography'. The wrong times come from adding 4 hours or 5 hours.
o: 11:00 a.m., in the Thar Desert
10:30 a.m., in the Thar Desert
11:00 a.m., still among the Aravalli Hills
11:30 a.m., in the Thar Desert

questions.q: Suppose the monsoon fails for a whole year in a Thar village. Which of the water practices in the chapter would still work, which would not, and what does this show about the way people have adapted to the desert?
questions.a: Scouring utensils with sand, using only a little water for a light rinse and reusing it for plants would still work, since they save water that is available. Taanka or kunds store rainwater, so they would stay empty if no rain fell. People adapt by combining saving habits with storage; the saving habits matter most when the rain fails.
s: Sand cleaning and light rinse still work
Rinse reuse for plants still works
Taanka or kunds depend on rain so would stay empty
Explains that habits save available water while storage needs rain
Concludes on how people adapt, linking to water scarcity

questions.q: True or False? 'Although a plateau has a more or less flat top, India's plateaus are home to many waterfalls, because rivers there flow over uneven and rocky surfaces.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A flat top does not mean a smooth river bed: the chapter says plateaus have many waterfalls as rivers flow over their uneven and rocky surfaces.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the river bed is uneven and rocky even though the top is flat

questions.q: A map reader sees a triangular upland with the Arabian Sea on its west, the Bay of Bengal on its east and the Indian Ocean at its southern tip. Her friend says, 'It must be an island because it has water around it.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter defines a peninsula as land surrounded by water on three sides. The upland meets the rest of the country on its fourth, northern side, so it is a peninsula, not an island.
o: It is a peninsula, because water bounds it on three sides only
It is an island, because the sea touches it on its sides
It is a peninsula, because the Ghats enclose it on two sides
It is an island, because the Indian Ocean lies beyond its tip

questions.q: Compare the Western Ghats and the Eastern Ghats and explain how the two ranges and the Deccan Plateau between them help to account for which way the plateau's rivers run.
questions.a: The Western Ghats are the taller range, running like a wall along the western coast with waterfalls in the monsoon. The Eastern Ghats are lower, broken into smaller hills along the eastern coast. Between them lies the Deccan Plateau, a vast area of flat highlands. The plateau tilts a little to the east, so rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi flow to the Bay of Bengal, while the Narmada and Tapti drain into the Arabian Sea.
s: Western Ghats: taller, wall-like, along the west
Eastern Ghats: lower and broken, along the east
Deccan Plateau between them
Tilt to the east and the east-flowing rivers
West-flowing Narmada and Tapti into the Arabian Sea

questions.q: A railway line runs from a port on the Arabian Sea coast to a port on the Bay of Bengal coast straight across the Peninsular Plateau. The number of mountain ranges it must cross is ___.

A state power board needs electricity all year and must choose one new plant. Plant H is a hydroelectric plant on a plateau waterfall river in the Western Ghats region, costing Rs 400 crore; the engineer says the river gives full power for only 5 months of the year. Plant C is a coal-fired plant near a plateau coal mine, costing Rs 300 crore, which runs all 12 months at the same capacity.
(a) Why does the Peninsular Plateau have so many waterfalls?
(b) What harm does the chapter link with coal?
(c) How much more does Plant H cost, and what share of Plant C's yearly output does Plant H give (to one decimal place)?
(d) Choose a plant, justify it with the figures, and name the cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Rivers flow over the uneven and rocky surfaces of the plateau. (b) Coal is a fossil fuel and its use contributes to global warming. (c) Rs 400 - 300 = Rs 100 crore more; 5/12 = 41.7 per cent of the yearly output. (d) Plant C gives full output for 12 months at Rs 100 crore less, but adds to global warming; Plant H avoids the fossil-fuel harm and also brings tourism and irrigation benefits, but costs Rs 100 crore more and supplies only about 42 per cent of the year. Either is acceptable if the cost named is the one of that choice.
s: Part (a): rivers over uneven rocky surfaces
Part (b): fossil fuel contributes to global warming
Part (c): Rs 100 crore more; 41.7 per cent
Part (d): a plant chosen with its cost named

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The dense forests of the plateau are home to tribal communities such as the Gond and the Bhil.
Reason (R): The plateau forests are the only places in India where tribal communities live.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the chapter lists tribal communities as spread over many states, including West Bengal, Assam and Gujarat, and the Khasi of the Northeast are another example.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A student writes: 'The plateau's coal mines give electricity without any harm, because coal is simply a natural resource of the plateau.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The Fig. 1.32 caption calls coal an important resource, especially for electricity, and a fossil fuel whose use contributes to global warming.
o: Coal is important for electricity, but it is a fossil fuel whose use contributes to global warming
Coal is harmless on the plateau, but harmful in the Himalayas
Coal is a renewable resource, so it is harmful only if mined too fast
Coal is not found on the plateau; the plateau's minerals are only waterfalls and forests

questions.q: Tanvi lists five rivers from the chapter - Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Narmada and Tapti - and says, 'Three of these five flow west.' Check her count and say what the chapter tells us about the direction of each.
questions.a: She is wrong. Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi are east-flowing, draining towards the Bay of Bengal, because the plateau tilts a little to the east. Only the Narmada and Tapti flow west into the Arabian Sea, so two flow west and three east.
s: Verdict: the count is wrong
Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi flow east to the Bay of Bengal
Narmada and Tapti flow west to the Arabian Sea, so two not three

questions.q: A mining company argues: 'The forest-dwelling communities of the plateau can live anywhere; their way of life has little to do with the forest.' (a) Rebut this with what the chapter says about their languages, traditions and ways of life. (b) Name three of the communities the chapter lists.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says these tribes have distinct languages, traditions and ways of life closely connected to Nature. (b) Any three of the Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil and Korku.
s: Part (a): distinct languages, traditions and ways of life closely connected to Nature
Part (b): three of Santhal, Gond, Baiga, Bhil, Korku

questions.q:
Match each feature of the Peninsular Plateau in Column A with the benefits the chapter gives for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. Coal mines  2. Waterfalls  3. East-flowing rivers such as the Godavari  4. Dense forests of Chhattisgarh
Column B: a. home to many tribal communities  b. production of electricity, though coal is a fossil fuel  c. tourists, hydroelectric power and water for irrigation  d. water for farming, industries and hydroelectric power
questions.a: Coal gives electricity but is a fossil fuel; waterfalls draw tourists, give hydroelectric power and irrigation water; the east-flowing rivers give water for farming, industries and hydroelectric power; the forests house tribal communities. The distractors swap waterfalls with the rivers.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Peninsular Plateau.
1. The Peninsular Plateau is a recent land formation.
2. East-flowing rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Mahanadi originate on the plateau.
3. The Deccan Plateau lies outside the Ghats, on the side facing the sea.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: the chapter calls the plateau a very old land formation. 3 is false: the Deccan Plateau lies between the two ranges. 2 is stated in the chapter.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: A newspaper calls the Peninsular Plateau 'vital for India's economy'. Give two points from the chapter in favour of the statement and one concern the chapter itself raises.
questions.a: In favour: it is rich in minerals, forests and fertile land; its rivers give water for farming and industries and for hydroelectric power; its waterfalls attract tourists and give power and irrigation water (any two). Concern: coal, an important source of electricity, is a fossil fuel whose use contributes to global warming.
s: First valid point in favour
Second valid point in favour
The concern: coal as a fossil fuel contributing to global warming

questions.q: A geography quiz describes four landforms. P: a low, flat stretch at the same level as the land around it. Q: a raised area with a more or less flat top and some steep sides. R: a narrow, pointed peak. S: a low hollow between two hills. Which one is a plateau by the chapter's definition?
questions.a: The chapter defines a plateau as a landform that rises up from the surrounding land with a more or less flat surface, some of its sides often steep slopes. P is a plain at the level of its surroundings, which is the common slip.
o: Q
P
R
S

questions.q: A guide says, 'Plateau waterfalls are only a tourist sight.' (a) Correct her with two further benefits from the chapter. (b) Why do rivers on a plateau, whose top is more or less flat, still form waterfalls?
questions.a: (a) They help in hydroelectric power generation and provide water for irrigation. (b) Rivers flow over the uneven and rocky surfaces of plateaus.
s: Part (a): hydroelectric power and irrigation water
Part (b): uneven, rocky surfaces make the rivers fall

questions.q: Compare the Peninsular Plateau and the Gangetic Plains under landform, rivers, resources and people, and analyse why the plateau forests are home to tribal communities while a large proportion of India's population lives on the plains.
questions.a: Landform: the plateau is raised, with a flat top and steep sides, and very old; the plains are flat. Rivers: the plateau's rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Mahanadi, Narmada, Tapti) rise on it and give water for farming, industry and power; the plains are watered by Himalayan rivers that bring minerals. Resources: the plateau is rich in minerals, forests and fertile land; the plains in fertile, mineral-rich soil. People: tribal communities with ways of life tied to Nature live in the dense plateau forests; a large proportion of India's population lives in the plains, where flat land, water and fertile soil support farming and roads and railways.
s: Landform contrast
River contrast
Resource contrast
People: tribal communities in forests, large population on plains
Analysis linking forest on the plateau and fertile flat land on the plains to the settlement pattern

questions.q: A river like the Godavari flows across the Peninsular Plateau from west to east. A boat set adrift on it at the western edge of the plateau drifts with the current to the sea. Which landforms does it pass, in order?
questions.a: The Deccan Plateau lies between the two ranges; the Eastern Ghats are along the eastern coast, and east-flowing rivers drain into the Bay of Bengal. The other orders reverse the landforms or send the river west.
o: The Deccan Plateau, then the Eastern Ghats, then the Bay of Bengal
The Eastern Ghats, then the Deccan Plateau, then the Bay of Bengal
The Deccan Plateau, then the Western Ghats, then the Arabian Sea
The Western Ghats, then the Eastern Ghats, then the Deccan Plateau

questions.q: Arun says, 'A plateau is flat, so there are no waterfalls on it, but its rivers still give water to millions.' Is he right? Give a verdict and support it from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly. He is right that the rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) are important for farming and give water to millions. He is wrong about waterfalls: rivers flow over the uneven, rocky surfaces of plateaus, so India's plateaus are home to many waterfalls.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: rivers give water to millions
Wrong part: uneven rocky surface gives many waterfalls

questions.q: A student says, 'The Western Ghats matter only for their waterfalls.' (a) Give two other reasons from the chapter why the range is important. (b) What other name does the chapter give to the northern portion of the range?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it is home to many rivers, it has a rich biodiversity. (b) The Sahyadri Hills.
s: Part (a): two valid reasons such as UNESCO site, many rivers or rich biodiversity
Part (b): the Sahyadri Hills

questions.q: (a) For which purpose does the chapter call the plateau's coal an especially important resource? (b) Name one benefit that plateau waterfalls give which coal cannot, and say why that matters for the harm the chapter links with coal.
questions.a: (a) The production of electricity. (b) Waterfalls give hydroelectric power without burning a fossil fuel (they also attract tourists and give irrigation water); coal is a fossil fuel whose use contributes to global warming.
s: Part (a): production of electricity
Part (b): hydroelectric power from waterfalls avoids the fossil-fuel harm of global warming

questions.q:
A Santhal village lives beside a dense plateau forest of 500 hectares. A company offers a coal mine that would clear 40 per cent of the forest and employ 300 villagers at Rs 10,000 a month each for ten years. The village's other option is a visitor trail to a waterfall inside the forest, which would employ 60 villagers at Rs 8,000 a month each and could run for ever.
(a) Name two other tribal communities of the plateau forests.
(b) How many hectares would the mine clear, and how many would remain?
(c) What are the total wages over ten years under each option?
(d) What should the gram sabha decide? Use the chapter's account of the forest and of coal in your answer.
questions.a: (a) Any two of the Gond, Baiga, Bhil, Korku. (b) 40 per cent of 500 = 200 hectares cleared, 300 remain. (c) Mine: 300 x 10,000 x 12 x 10 = Rs 36 crore. Trail: 60 x 8,000 x 12 x 10 = Rs 5.76 crore. (d) The mine pays about six times as much over ten years but clears 200 hectares of the forest to which these communities' ways of life are closely connected, and coal is a fossil fuel that contributes to global warming; the trail pays less but keeps the forest and could continue after ten years. Either choice is acceptable if the gram sabha names what it gives up.
s: Part (a): two other tribal communities
Part (b): 200 hectares cleared and 300 remain
Part (c): Rs 36 crore and Rs 5.76 crore
Part (d): a decision using the forest tie and the coal harm, with the loss named

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The west coast and the east coast of India are alike, with wide plains and big deltas on both.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. The west coast, from Gujarat to Kerala, has short, swift rivers from the Western Ghats forming estuaries, with the Western Ghats close to the sea. The east coast, between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal, has wide plains and deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri.
s: Verdict: disagrees
West coast: swift short rivers forming estuaries
East coast: wide plains and major deltas

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the term the chapter uses for it in Column B.
Column A: 1. A short, swift river from the Western Ghats meets the Arabian Sea  2. The Godavari deposits sediments to build fan-shaped land at its mouth  3. Pulicat, a body of water cut off from the Bay of Bengal by a natural barrier  4. The 36 coral islands of Lakshadweep
Column B: a. estuary  b. delta  c. lagoon  d. archipelago
questions.a: A west-coast river forms an estuary; the Godavari forms a delta; Pulicat is a lagoon; Lakshadweep is an archipelago, a group of islands. The distractors swap estuary with delta, or lagoon with archipelago.

questions.q: In her notebook Pooja labels the mouth of the Godavari 'lagoon' and Pulicat Lake 'delta'. Which correction matches the chapter?
questions.a: A delta is the triangular or fan-shaped land a river builds at its mouth from sediments, as at the Godavari. A lagoon is a body of water separated from larger waters by a natural barrier, as at Pulicat.
o: The Godavari mouth is a delta; Pulicat is a lagoon
Both are deltas, since both lie on the east coast
The Godavari mouth is a lagoon; Pulicat is an estuary
Both are lagoons, since both hold water near the sea

questions.q: A satellite image shows a coast with a wide plain, fan-shaped fertile land where a river meets the sea, and a large lake lying behind a natural barrier. Which coast does the chapter describe in this way?
questions.a: The chapter gives the east coast wide plains, major river deltas and lakes such as Chilika and Pulicat. The west coast has coves, creeks and estuaries.
o: The east coast, between the Eastern Ghats and the Bay of Bengal
The west coast, between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea
The coast of the Lakshadweep islands, made of coral
The coast of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, made of volcanic islands

questions.q:
A school in Visakhapatnam has Rs 1,50,000 for a trip for 45 students on the theme 'Where rivers meet the sea: land and livelihood'. It can visit only one coast. The west-coast plan covers the Narmada and Tapti estuaries and the port city of Mumbai at Rs 3,200 per student. The east-coast plan covers the Godavari delta and Chilika Lake at Rs 2,100 per student.
(a) How does a river build a delta, and how is the coast of the swift west-coast rivers different?
(b) What does the chapter say each coast offers people?
(c) What does each plan cost for 45 students, and how much of the grant is left?
(d) Choose a plan, justify it against the theme, and say what the school gives up.
questions.a: (a) A delta forms where a river deposits sediments at its mouth, building a triangular or fan-shaped area; the swift west-coast rivers from the Western Ghats form estuaries, with coves and creeks. (b) West: important ports and cities, centres of economic activity for millennia, with Mumbai the financial centre. East: wide plains and fertile deltas ideal for farming, and lakes like Chilika and Pulicat. (c) West: 45 x 3,200 = Rs 1,44,000, leaving Rs 6,000; east: 45 x 2,100 = Rs 94,500, leaving Rs 55,500. (d) West covers the livelihood of trade and ports but spends nearly the whole grant and gives up the farming delta; east shows land and farming and leaves Rs 55,500 but gives up the port city. Either is acceptable if the loss is named.
s: Part (a): delta from deposited sediments; swift rivers form estuaries
Part (b): west ports and cities; east fertile deltas and farming
Part (c): Rs 1,44,000 and Rs 94,500; Rs 6,000 and Rs 55,500 left
Part (d): a plan chosen against the theme with the loss named

questions.q:
Study the statements about India's coasts and islands.
1. Lakshadweep, in the Bay of Bengal, is made up of 36 coral islands.
2. About one-third of the Sundarbans delta is in India and the rest is in Bangladesh.
3. Barren Island, in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, is the only active volcano in India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 is false: Lakshadweep lies in the Arabian Sea. 2 is false: about half of the delta is in India. 3 is stated in the chapter.
o: 3 only
1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A large dam is built on a river upstream of its delta and traps most of the sediments the river carries. (a) According to the chapter, what is a delta built from? (b) Predict what happens to the build-up of the delta and to the farming it supports, giving your reason.
questions.a: (a) Sediments that the river deposits at its mouth into a larger body of water, building a triangular or fan-shaped area. (b) With fewer sediments arriving, less new land would build up and the delta's fertile land would be renewed less, so farming on it would suffer.
s: Part (a): sediments deposited by the river at its mouth
Part (b): fewer sediments, less build-up and less fertile land, so farming suffers, with the reason

questions.q: India's coastline is over 7500 km long. A cycling team plans to ride the whole coastline at 125 km a day with no rest day. How many days will it need, going by the chapter's figure?
questions.a: 7500 / 125 = 60, and the coastline is over 7500 km, so the ride needs more than 60 days. The other figures come from slips of a decimal place or a halving.
o: More than 60 days
About 6 days
About 30 days
More than 600 days

questions.q: Mawlynnong in the East Khasi Hills is called 'the cleanest village in Asia'. (a) Name two practices the chapter gives for it. (b) How do the Khasi festival Shad Suk Mynsiem and the living root bridges express the same attitude to Nature that these practices do?
questions.a: (a) Well-maintained cleanliness, bamboo dustbins and eco-friendly living (any two). (b) The festival is a form of gratitude towards nature, and the root bridges are made by weaving tree roots over many years, working with nature; like the clean-village practices, they show care for and respect towards the environment.
s: Part (a): two practices such as bamboo dustbins and eco-friendly living
Part (b): the festival as gratitude towards nature
Part (b): the root bridges woven from living roots, showing the same respect for Nature

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sundarbans lie entirely within India.
Reason (R): The Sundarbans are located in the delta of the Ganga, the Brahmaputra and their tributaries.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: about half is in India and the rest in Bangladesh. R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: True or False? 'The Godavari and the Narmada both flow into the sea, yet the Godavari builds a delta at its mouth while the Narmada forms an estuary.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says east-coast rivers such as the Godavari deposit sediments to build fertile deltas, while the rivers of the west coast, such as the Narmada and Tapti, rise in the Western Ghats, flow swiftly and form estuaries.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: east-coast rivers deposit sediments to form deltas; swift west-coast rivers form estuaries

questions.q: Two students compare India's island groups. Asha: 'Both Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are volcanic and lie in the Bay of Bengal.' Bilal: 'Lakshadweep is made of coral and lies in the Arabian Sea; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are volcanic and lie in the Bay of Bengal.' Whose statement matches the chapter?
